section.title: Parametric surfaces and tangent planes
section.p: A curve needed one parameter: \mathbf r(t). A surface needs two. One parameter moves along one family of curves on the surface; the other moves along a crossing family. Together they form a coordinate grid on the surface.

subsection.title: Two parameters make a surface
subsection.p: Think of a rectangular sheet of rubber. Before it is bent, a point on the sheet can be labeled by two numbers: (u,v). After the sheet is bent into space, the point has three coordinates: (x,y,z). So a bent sheet is naturally described by a function \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)).
The input (u,v) lives in a flat parameter region. The output \mathbf r(u,v) lives in space.

statement.p: A surface lives in three-dimensional space, yet we describe it using only two parameters (u,v). Why two and not three? What does this say about how a surface sits inside space?

hint.p: Think about how many directions you can actually walk while staying on the rubber sheet, before it is bent or after.

subsection.p: For example, a cylinder of radius 2 can be described by \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,\,2\sin\theta,\,z), where 0\le \theta\le 2\pi, \qquad 0\le z\le 5. The parameter \theta moves around the cylinder. The parameter z moves upward.

If \theta=\pi/3 and z=4, then \mathbf r\left(\frac{\pi}{3},4\right) = \left(1,\sqrt3,4\right). So the flat rectangle 0\le \theta\le 2\pi,\qquad 0\le z\le5 has been wrapped into the side of a cylinder.

statement.p: A parametric surface in space is a function \mathbf r:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3 of the form \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)). The set \{\mathbf r(u,v):(u,v)\in D\} is the image of the parametrization.

subsection.p: The parameters do not have to be called u and v. On a cylinder, it is more natural to use \theta and z. On a sphere, it is more natural to use two angles.

subsection.title: Coordinate curves on a surface
subsection.p: A parametrized surface comes with two families of curves.

For the cylinder \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), hold z fixed and let \theta vary. We get a horizontal circle: \theta\longmapsto (2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z_0). Hold \theta fixed and let z vary. We get a vertical line: z\longmapsto (2\cos\theta_0,2\sin\theta_0,z).
These two curve families form the grid on the surface.

statement.p: For the cylinder \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), differentiate with respect to \theta: \mathbf r_\theta(\theta,z)=(-2\sin\theta,2\cos\theta,0). This points around the cylinder.
Differentiate with respect to z: \mathbf r_z(\theta,z)=(0,0,1). This points straight upward.

At \theta=\frac{\pi}{3},\qquad z=2, the point on the cylinder is \mathbf r\left(\frac{\pi}{3},2\right) = (1,\sqrt3,2). The two tangent directions are \mathbf r_\theta\left(\frac{\pi}{3},2\right) = (-\sqrt3,1,0) and \mathbf r_z\left(\frac{\pi}{3},2\right) = (0,0,1). One direction goes around the pipe. The other goes up the pipe.

Let \mathbf r(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)). Assume its first partial derivatives exist. The two coordinate tangent vectors are \boxed{ \mathbf r_u=(x_u,y_u,z_u), \qquad \mathbf r_v=(x_v,y_v,z_v). } They are tangent to the coordinate curves obtained by holding one parameter fixed.

subsection.p: Independent coordinate tangent vectors describe two local directions of a sheet. Dependent vectors signal a defect in this parametrization; they do not by themselves prove that the geometric surface has a singularity.

subsection.title: Normal direction from the cross product
subsection.p: Two nonparallel tangent vectors determine a plane. A normal vector to that plane is given by their cross product: \mathbf r_u\times \mathbf r_v.

For the cylinder, \mathbf r_\theta=(-2\sin\theta,2\cos\theta,0), \qquad \mathbf r_z=(0,0,1). So
\mathbf r_\theta\times \mathbf r_z \amp= (2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,0).
This vector points radially outward. At \theta=\pi/3, \mathbf r_\theta\times \mathbf r_z=(1,\sqrt3,0). That is exactly the outward normal direction at the point (1,\sqrt3,z).

figure.caption: The two parameter directions on a cylinder give two tangent directions \mathbf r_\theta (around) and \mathbf r_z (up); their cross product \mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z is the outward normal. Arrows show directions and are scaled for visibility. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

image.shortdescription: A cylinder with two coordinate tangent directions and their outward cross product at one point.

subsection.p: The order matters. If we reverse the order, \mathbf r_z\times \mathbf r_\theta = -(\mathbf r_\theta\times \mathbf r_z), so the normal points inward instead of outward. This sign will become part of orientation and flux later.

statement.p: Swapping \mathbf r_u\times \mathbf r_v for \mathbf r_v\times \mathbf r_u flips the normal to the other side of the surface. Geometrically, the surface itself has not changed at all. So what extra piece of information are we choosing when we pick an order for the cross product?

hint.p: The surface is the same either way, but you select which normal direction counts as positive. An arbitrary patch need not have an inside or an outside.

statement.p: A parametrization \mathbf r(u,v) is called smooth if its first partial derivatives are continuous.

It is called regular at (u,v) if \boxed{ \mathbf r_u(u,v)\times \mathbf r_v(u,v)\ne \mathbf 0. } At an interior parameter point, a smooth regular map describes a smooth sheet after restricting to a sufficiently small neighborhood. To justify the local-sheet claim, a nonzero component of the cross product is a nonzero 2\times2 minor of the derivative. Project onto those two output coordinates. The inverse function theorem from gives local inverse coordinates, in which the third output coordinate is a C^1 graph. Distinct parameter neighborhoods may still meet in the image; the tangent plane belongs to the selected local sheet.

exercise.title: What do the two tangents build?

statement.p: Holding v fixed and varying u gives one grid curve; holding u fixed and varying v gives another. Why does this produce two tangent vectors \mathbf r_u and \mathbf r_v at a point, and at a regular point, what geometric object does their cross product \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v describe?

hint.p: Each parameter direction traces its own curve through the point, and each curve has its own tangent. Recall that a cross product is perpendicular to both factors. If \mathbf r_u and \mathbf r_v both lie in its tangent plane, where must \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v point?

subsection.p: The regularity condition says that the two parameter directions really make a little surface patch, not just a curve or a point.

subsection.title: Tangent planes to parametrized surfaces
subsection.p: At an interior point of a smooth regular patch, the tangent plane is spanned by \mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0). If \mathbf p=\mathbf r(u_0,v_0), then a parametric equation for the tangent plane is \boxed{ \mathbf X=\mathbf p+s\,\mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0)+t\,\mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0). } A normal vector is \mathbf n=\mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0)\times \mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0), so the same plane can be written as \boxed{ \mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf X-\mathbf p)=0. }

theorem.title: Tangent plane to a parametrized surface

statement.p: Let \mathbf r:D\to\mathbb R^3 be smooth on a neighborhood of an interior point (u_0,v_0) and regular there. Set \mathbf p=\mathbf r(u_0,v_0). Then the tangent plane to this local sheet at \mathbf p is \boxed{ \mathbf X=\mathbf p+s\,\mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0)+t\,\mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0). } Equivalently, if \mathbf n=\mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0)\times \mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0), then \boxed{ \mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf X-\mathbf p)=0. }

proof.p: The curve u\longmapsto \mathbf r(u,v_0) lies on the surface, and its velocity at u=u_0 is \mathbf r_u(u_0,v_0). So \mathbf r_u is tangent to the surface.
Similarly, the curve v\longmapsto \mathbf r(u_0,v) lies on the surface, and its velocity at v=v_0 is \mathbf r_v(u_0,v_0). So \mathbf r_v is also tangent.

By the local linear approximation in , \mathbf r(u_0+h,v_0+k)=\mathbf p+h\mathbf r_u+k\mathbf r_v+\mathbf E(h,k), \qquad \frac{\|\mathbf E(h,k)\|}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}\longrightarrow0. Thus this plane approximates all nearby parameter displacements to first order, not just the two coordinate curves. Regularity makes it a plane rather than a line; the cross product is normal to it.

example.title: A tangent plane to a cylinder

statement.p: For the cylinder \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), take \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}, \qquad z=4. Then \mathbf p=(1,\sqrt3,4). The tangent vectors are \mathbf r_\theta=(-\sqrt3,1,0), \qquad \mathbf r_z=(0,0,1). A normal vector is \mathbf n=\mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z=(1,\sqrt3,0). Therefore the tangent plane is (1,\sqrt3,0)\cdot\bigl((x,y,z)-(1,\sqrt3,4)\bigr)=0. That is x-1+\sqrt3(y-\sqrt3)=0, or \boxed{ x+\sqrt3\,y=4. } The tangent plane is vertical, as it should be for the side of a cylinder.

subsection.title: Graphs as parametrized surfaces
subsection.p: This agrees with the tangent-plane formula from . If \mathbf p=(a,b,g(a,b)), then z-g(a,b)=g_x(a,b)(x-a)+g_y(a,b)(y-b).

example.title: A tangent plane to a curved shade cloth

statement.p: A shade cloth over a courtyard has height g(x,y)=4+\frac{x}{3}-\frac{y}{4}-\frac{x^2}{12}. At the point (x,y)=(1,2), the height is g(1,2) = 4+\frac13-\frac12-\frac1{12} = \frac{15}{4}. The partial derivatives are g_x(x,y)=\frac13-\frac{x}{6}, \qquad g_y(x,y)=-\frac14. At (1,2), g_x(1,2)=\frac16, \qquad g_y(1,2)=-\frac14. So the tangent plane is \boxed{ z-\frac{15}{4} = \frac16(x-1)-\frac14(y-2). } In parametric-surface language, this is the same plane spanned by \mathbf r_x=\left(1,0,\frac16\right), \qquad \mathbf r_y=\left(0,1,-\frac14\right).

subsection.title: Why the hypotheses matter
subsection.p: We asked for smoothness and regularity because tangent planes can fail in two different ways.

First, a surface can have a crease. Consider z=|x|. A natural parametrization is \mathbf r(x,y)=(x,y,|x|). Along the line x=0, the surface folds like a roof ridge. Approaching from x>0, the surface has slope +1 in the x-direction. Approaching from x<0, it has slope -1. There is no single tangent plane along the crease.
The partial derivative with respect to x does not exist there. Smoothness was not a decoration; it prevented a hidden fold.

example.title: Why regularity matters: the tip of a cone

statement.p: The upper cone z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} has the parametrization \mathbf r(s,\theta) = (s\cos\theta,s\sin\theta,s), \qquad s\ge0,\quad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. For s\gt0, the parameters describe points away from the tip.

At the tip, s=0, all angles give the same point: \mathbf r(0,\theta)=(0,0,0). The tangent directions are \mathbf r_s=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,1), and \mathbf r_\theta=(-s\sin\theta,s\cos\theta,0). At s=0, \mathbf r_\theta=(0,0,0). So \mathbf r_s\times\mathbf r_\theta=\mathbf 0. The parametrization is not regular at the tip.

Geometrically, this matches what we see. The cone has a sharp point. The three straight generators with directions (1,0,1), (-1,0,1), and (0,1,1) all reach the tip. Their determinant is -2, so they do not lie in one plane. Thus no single tangent plane can contain all three directions.

subsection.p: Failure of regularity alone does not settle the geometry. The spherical coordinates of collapse at a pole, but near the north pole the same sphere has the regular graph patch \mathbf q(u,v)=(u,v,\sqrt{9-u^2-v^2}),\qquad u^2+v^2\lt9. At (0,0) its coordinate tangent vectors are (1,0,0) and (0,1,0). The sphere therefore has a tangent plane there. The cone's three independent generator directions, rather than merely a zero cross product, rule out a plane at its tip.

exercise.title: A coordinate defect or a sharp tip?

statement.p: Both the cone coordinates and the spherical coordinates have a zero cross product at a collapsed edge. Why does this fact alone not decide whether the image has a tangent plane? What additional argument distinguishes the cone?

hint.p: Use the regular graph patch for the sphere and the three independent generator directions for the cone.

subsection.p: So a smooth regular patch is the surface version of a smooth curve with nonzero velocity. It has a well-defined tangent plane and a normal direction.

But a normal direction is not yet an area. The vector \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v does two jobs at once: it points perpendicular to the surface, and its length measures how much a tiny parameter rectangle has been stretched. That length is the next piece of the story.
